name: Duke Energy Corporation
employees: ~26,000 at December 31, 2025 (Q4 2025 investor presentation, company overview slide)
summary: BOTTOM LINE UP FRONT: Duke Energy has the corpus's most conservatively reported data-center book — ~7.8 GW of signed electric service agreements at the August 4, 2026 call, ~5.2 GW under construction and a ~15.4 GW 'high-confidence, late-stage pipeline' it expects to convert by the first half of 2027 — and it is building the largest regulated gas fleet in this file against it (7,501 MW across seven plants with 26 GE Vernova turbines secured) alongside ~4.5 GW of utility-owned batteries by 2031, inside a $103B 2026–2030 plan that is 39 percent grid; the terms on which those loads connect are still being written, in a North Carolina large-load tariff proceeding due before January 1, 2027, a Florida large-load policy the state commission has called 'facially noncompliant', and an Ohio Rate DC filing, and on September 18–19, 2026 the North Carolina Utilities Commission denied the company's first data-center-justified gas turbine, a 255 MW peaker, for load 'never tested in contested proceedings'. BACKGROUND. Charlotte, North Carolina; NYSE: DUK. Six electric utilities — Duke Energy Carolinas and Duke Energy Progress (to be combined January 1, 2027), Duke Energy Florida, Duke Energy Indiana, Duke Energy Ohio and Duke Energy Kentucky — serve about 8.7 million customers with 55,700 MW of capacity, and Piedmont Natural Gas about 1.6 million after the Tennessee business was sold to Spire for $2.48B on March 31, 2026. Brookfield Super-Core Infrastructure Partners bought the first 9.2 percent of a 19.7 percent, $6B minority stake in Duke Energy Florida's parent on March 3, 2026 ($2.8B), with the balance due in four tranches through June 2028 — the coverage plan's 'first closing not confirmed' was wrong. FY2025 adjusted EPS was $6.31 on revenue of $32,237M; 2026 guidance of $6.55–$6.80 was reaffirmed in August with 5–7 percent growth through 2030, funded by $10B of common equity over 2027–2030. Collection gap: www.duke-energy.com returned 403 to this network on every path, so leadership bios, the 2026 Carolinas Resource Plan chapters, the Indiana IRP and the tariff sheets were read through filings, regulators' sites and trade press; SEC's Archives were reachable for the 8-Ks but the FY2025 10-K narrative was not read; no battery supplier is named in any source; and the Q3 2026 earnings date is unconfirmed by the company (trackers give October 29, November 5 and November 6).
ecosystemRole: We assess Duke Energy as the utility whose data-center exposure is spread across the most jurisdictions in this corpus — five state commissions, two RTOs and two non-RTO regions — and whose disclosed pipeline is therefore the least inflated: it reports signed ESAs and construction, not inquiries, and its 7.8 GW compares with 53.8 GW at Dominion and 69 GW at AEP only because those companies count earlier rungs. Basis: the three 2026 investor presentations and the Q2 2026 call. For the storage sellers in this file Duke is a self-build buyer with an undisclosed supplier and three doors — the Carolinas resource-plan batteries at retiring coal sites (Allen, Riverbend, Knightdale), Duke Energy Florida's solar-sited and transmission-tied batteries (Powerline 2027, Bartow 2028), and the South Carolina 400 MW standalone storage RFP — and for the gas and grid vendors it is GE Vernova's largest disclosed utility turbine customer (26 units) and a $1B-a-year North Carolina supply-chain buyer (GE Vernova Goldsboro transformers, Siemens Energy Charlotte). For the developers and hyperscalers in the corpus it is the counterparty to Microsoft (Person and Catawba Counties), Amazon (Richmond County), QTS (York County), Compass and Digital Realty, and the utility whose 'Customer Protection Plus' terms — customer-funded connection, minimum bills, termination charges, curtailment for up to 50 hours a year — are being turned into tariffs in North Carolina, Florida and Ohio during the fourth quarter of 2026.

productsAndServices.name: Regulated retail electric service — six utilities in six states, and the large-load contract framework
productsAndServices.description: Duke Energy's electric utilities — Duke Energy Carolinas and Duke Energy Progress (North and South Carolina), Duke Energy Florida, Duke Energy Indiana, Duke Energy Ohio and Duke Energy Kentucky — serve about 8.7 million customers and own about 55,700 MW of generating capacity (56 GW winter rating at December 31, 2025), per the Q2 2026 results release and the Q4 2025 investor presentation. The Carolinas and Florida utilities are vertically integrated and sit outside any RTO (SERC and FRCC reliability regions); Duke Energy Indiana is in MISO; Duke Energy Ohio is a wires-only company inside PJM under an electric security plan through May 2028, and Duke Energy Kentucky owns generation in PJM. Rates are set by five state commissions: the NCUC and PSCSC (the North Carolina multiyear rate plans filed November 20, 2025 settled in July and August 2026 at a 9.8 percent return on equity, with orders expected in mid-November 2026 and rates from January 1, 2027), the Florida PSC (a 2025–2027 multiyear settlement), the IURC (Indiana's HEA 1002 multiyear framework) and the PUCO (electric case 26-0132-EL-AIR filed March 30, 2026). Large-load terms are being written state by state. In North Carolina, Duke's rate-case proposal (Canary Media, July 2026) sets a 50 MW threshold, a minimum bill of 75 percent of maximum potential demand and 10–15-year terms with termination charges; advocates and the Public Staff want 25 MW, 85 percent, 20 years and a separate class, and both NC settlements commit to a separate, expedited large-load tariff proceeding to finish before rates take effect on January 1, 2027. In Florida, Duke Energy Florida's Large Load Customer Policy (FPSC Docket 20260064-EI, refiled April 22, 2026 under SB 484) applies at 50 MW with a 20-year minimum term, take-or-pay of 75–85 percent of contracted capacity, a termination fee of three years of minimum bills plus the net book value of dedicated facilities, 100 percent of extension cost advanced as refundable CIAC, and no rate schedule until the next rate case — the Office of Public Counsel and Commissioner La Rosa called it 'facially noncompliant' at the August 25–26 hearing and a written order is pending. Duke Energy Ohio has proposed a Rate DC data-center tariff (PUCO 26-0755-EL-ATA); South Carolina opened a generic large-load docket (2026-138-E) after service-regulation updates for loads of 50 MW or more.
highlights: Large-load contract provisions the company lists on every 2026 investor deck: long-term contract, minimum billing demand, credit support, termination damages, refundable capital advance and an interruptibility provision — 'detailed contract provisions may vary across service territories'

'Customer Protection Plus' (July 23, 2026): engineering studies before connection; long-term agreements with customer-funded connection costs, upfront financial security, termination charges and temporary curtailment for targeted grid events; revenue sharing when large-load revenues exceed the cost to serve

Duke Energy Progress is to be merged into Duke Energy Carolinas effective January 1, 2027, with FERC, NCUC and PSCSC approvals received by May 2026 and an estimated $2.3B of net customer savings over 2027–2040
Retail load growth guidance: 1.5–2 percent in 2026 and 3–4 percent a year over 2027–2030 for the enterprise; ~2 percent and 4–5 percent for the Carolinas

Florida large-load policy (Docket 20260064-EI): ≥50 MW, 20-year term, 75–85 percent take-or-pay, three-year termination fee plus net book value, CIAC advanced in full and refunded over five years, $150,000 system-impact-study fee, no service to foreign-entity large loads
productsAndServices.positioning: Against Dominion Energy Virginia's GS-5 class (14-year terms, 85/60 percent minimums from 2027) and AEP's eight commission-approved large-load tariffs, Duke's protections are written contract-by-contract inside electric service agreements rather than as one published rate class — the decks say provisions 'may vary across service territories'. The Florida proposal's 20-year term is the longest in the corpus; its absence of a rate schedule is what the Florida PSC is testing against SB 484.

productsAndServices.name: Large-load interconnection — the pipeline ladder from late-stage prospect to electric service agreement to construction
productsAndServices.description: Duke reports its data-center business on a three-rung ladder: a 'high-confidence, late-stage pipeline', signed electric service agreements (ESAs), and load under construction. Per the investor presentations, signed data-center ESAs moved from about 3 GW at the November 2025 call to ~4.5 GW (February 10, 2026), ~7.6 GW (May 5, 2026, including contract volume signed in 2024) and ~7.8 GW (August 4, 2026); about 5.2 GW of data centers were under construction in August 2026 and the late-stage pipeline stood at ~15.4 GW on both 2026 decks. The Q2 2026 deck adds $5–10B of potential capital to serve large loads in Indiana and Florida that is not in the $103B plan. Named sites in Duke's own materials are the substation serving Microsoft's data center in Catawba County, North Carolina, Amazon's data-center site in Richmond County, North Carolina, and QTS's site in York County, South Carolina; a May 2024 agreement with Amazon, Google, Microsoft and Nucor created the Accelerating Clean Energy and Clean Transition tariff concepts for new nuclear and long-duration storage. Duke publishes no inquiry-stage gigawatt figure.

~5.2 GW of data centers under construction and a ~15.4 GW high-confidence late-stage pipeline at the Q2 2026 call

productsAndServices.name: Dispatchable generation build — more than 7.5 GW of new gas and ~15 GW of capacity by 2031
productsAndServices.description: The 'all-of-the-above' build on the Q2 2026 investor presentation adds about 15 GW of capacity by 2031 (raised from ~14 GW in February), including uprates of more than 1 GW (gas ~670 MW, nuclear ~250 MW, hydro ~85 MW) and 7,501 MW of new gas: Person County CC1 (North Carolina, 1,360 MW, CPCN approved, in service year-end 2028), Marshall CT 1 and 2 (850 MW, approved, 2028), Person County CC2 (1,360 MW, approved, 2029), Cayuga CC 1 and 2 (Indiana, 1,476 MW, approved, 2029/2030, ground broken May 14, 2026), Buck CT 3 and 4 (850 MW, CPCN requested, 2029), Smith CT (240 MW, requested, 2029) and Anderson County CC (South Carolina, ~1,365 MW, certified by the PSCSC on March 26, 2026, in service early 2031). Construction is under way on about 5 GW in the Carolinas and Indiana with EPC contracts signed for the first ~5 GW and gas supply contracted for every announced plant. GE Vernova is the turbine supplier — 19 units at the November 2025 call, 20 in February and May 2026, 26 by August 2026 — with the first Person County turbine delivered in July 2026 from the Greenville, South Carolina factory. The 2025 Carolinas Resource Plan's near-term action plan carries five combined-cycle units (6,825 MW) and seven combustion turbines (2,825 MW) by 2033.

productsAndServices.name: Battery storage — ~4.5 GW online by 2031, utility-owned on retired coal sites and at solar plants
productsAndServices.description: Every 2026 investor deck states that Duke is 'accelerating battery storage development, with ~4.5 GW of capacity online by 2031', and the Q2 2026 construction table carries a 'Battery Storage Portfolio' of ~4,500 MW across North Carolina, South Carolina, Florida and Indiana for 2026–2030 in active construction, regulatory approval or development. The 2025 Carolinas Resource Plan (filed October 1, 2025) plans 5,600 MW of battery storage in service by 2034 (2,900 MW more than the 2023 plan) sited at retiring coal plants including Allen, Riverbend and Mayo; the January 2026 Allen release cites 6,550 MW of batteries across the Carolinas by 2035, and the North Carolina rate cases include $1.7B of battery storage and about $400M of solar paired with storage for 2027–2028. Named projects: Allen BESS 1 — 50 MW, four hours, ~$100M, at the former Allen coal plant in Belmont, North Carolina, online November 2025 'under budget and ahead of schedule'; Allen BESS 2 — 167 MW, four hours, construction from May 2026, the company's largest; Riverbend BESS — 115 MW, Mount Holly, construction late 2026, online late 2027; Knightdale BESS — 100 MW; in Florida, Powerline (100 MW, more than 200 MWh, 2027) and Bartow (225 MW, 2028) in the 2026 Ten-Year Site Plan, plus a 5 MW, eight-hour sodium-sulfur battery at Suwannee and 50–75 MW batteries at solar sites; a 400 MW standalone storage RFP in South Carolina under the 2026 resource plan. Duke Energy Florida plans 1.4 GW of storage over ten years with more than $500M of investment tax credits. No battery supplier is named in any 2025–2026 Duke release; the company is testing EnerVenue nickel-hydrogen, Eos zinc and GKN hydrogen storage. 175 MW of storage entered service in 2025.
highlights: ~4.5 GW of battery storage online by 2031 (all three 2026 investor presentations); 5,600 MW in the Carolinas by 2034 (2025 CRP)
Allen BESS 1 (50 MW) online November 2025; Allen 2 (167 MW) and Riverbend (115 MW) under construction 2026; a third Allen battery proposed by end-2028

productsAndServices.name: Nuclear fleet — 10,773 MW, subsequent license renewals, uprates and the 2037 new-nuclear option
productsAndServices.description: Eleven units at six plants (Brunswick 1,870 MW, Harris 964 MW, McGuire 2,316 MW, Catawba 2,310 MW, Oconee 2,554 MW, Robinson 759 MW) ran at a record 96.9 percent capacity factor in 2025, the 27th consecutive year above 90 percent, and generated about $600M of nuclear production tax credits that flowed to customers (company release, February 20, 2026). The NRC granted Oconee's subsequent license renewal to 2053–2054 on March 31, 2025 and Robinson's to 2050 in April 2026; the Brunswick application is due by end-2026 and the company intends to renew all eleven units. About 300 MW of uprates are planned at four stations (~250 MW by 2031). For new nuclear, Duke filed an early site permit for Belews Creek, Stokes County, North Carolina on December 30, 2025 (permit expected 2027; four SMR and two non-light-water designs under consideration; first SMR targeted 2036, 600 MW by 2037), holds the W.S. Lee site in Cherokee County, South Carolina for a large reactor, collaborates with TVA on the DOE-funded BWRX-300 program, and signed 2024 agreements with Amazon, Google, Microsoft and Nucor to fund such projects through tariffs. The NCUC's 2024 order approved $440M of new-nuclear development spending toward 300 MW by 2034 and 600 MW by 2035.
highlights: Record 96.9 percent fleet capacity factor in 2025; ~$600M of nuclear PTCs to customers; nuclear fuel ~$3.2B in the 2026–2030 plan
Oconee renewed to 2053/2054 (March 2025); Robinson to 2050 (April 2026); Brunswick filing by end-2026
Belews Creek early site permit filed December 30, 2025, decision expected 2027; 'maintaining optionality for new nuclear to be online by 2037'
Up to $3.1B of nuclear, solar and storage tax credits generated 2025–2028 sold under a transfer agreement announced May 4, 2026
productsAndServices.positioning: The second-largest regulated nuclear fleet in the United States after Southern Nuclear's by unit count is Duke's, and unlike Constellation's merchant fleet its output is rate-based; the new-nuclear timetable (2036–2037) matches Dominion's North Anna SMR horizon.
productsAndServices.soldThrough: Regulated generation in rate base; tax credits monetized through transfer agreements
targetSegments: Hyperscalers willing to fund advanced nuclear through the ACE and CTT tariff structures
productsAndServices.roadmap: Brunswick SLR application by end-2026; Belews Creek ESP decision 2027; SMR design selection not yet announced

productsAndServices.name: Transmission and distribution — the largest T&D system in the United States and ~39 percent of the capital plan
productsAndServices.description: About 320,000 miles of transmission and distribution lines; grid investment is ~39 percent of the $103B 2026–2030 plan and ~40 percent of the $200–220B ten-year plan (Q4 2025 investor presentation). Federal support in 2026: a $50M DOE SPARK selection (September 24, 2026) for advanced conductors and dynamic line ratings in Greenville and Spartanburg, South Carolina and Henderson and Polk, North Carolina ($201M total project cost); about $96M of Defense Production Act grants for coal-plant refurbishment at East Bend, Roxboro and Belews Creek (June 5, 2026); and DOE loan applications (May 11, 2026) the company says could save customers 'potentially billions'. About $1B of North Carolina and ~$600M of South Carolina storm costs were securitized in 2025. Duke's 2025 spend with North Carolina suppliers was about $1B, including GE Vernova's Goldsboro transformer plant and Siemens Energy's Charlotte facility, and could reach $5B over five years (June 30, 2026).
highlights: Grid ~39 percent of $103B (2026–2030); ~40 percent of the ten-year plan
DOE SPARK $50M for advanced conductors and dynamic line ratings in the Carolinas (September 2026)
~$1.6B of storm-cost securitization bonds in 2025
Substations built for named data centers — Microsoft, Catawba County (deck photo caption)
productsAndServices.positioning: Duke's grid program is distribution-heavy and state-regulated; it has no 765 kV backbone comparable to AEP's and, outside Ohio and Kentucky, no FERC-formula transmission rate — the Carolinas and Florida recover transmission through retail rates.
productsAndServices.soldThrough: Rate base under retail rate cases; storm securitization
productsAndServices.roadmap: DOE loan decisions pending; SPARK projects to be built over the plan period

productsAndServices.name: Solar and renewable procurement — 4,000 MW by 2034 in the Carolinas, Florida self-build, Indiana
productsAndServices.description: The 2025 Carolinas Resource Plan carries 4,000 MW of new solar by 2034 through annual competitive procurement; the 2024 NCUC order had set 3,460 MW of solar and 1,100 MW of storage by 2031 and 1,200 MW of onshore wind with 300 MW by 2031, and waived the 70 percent-by-2030 interim carbon target. Duke Energy Florida self-builds solar under its 2024 rate settlement (more than 900 MW pre-approved for 2025–early 2028, then 375 MW in 2028 rising to 600 MW a year after 2030 per the 2026 Ten-Year Site Plan), completing the Sumter County site on May 21, 2026 and unveiling the Rattler Renewable Energy Center with FAMU on May 8, 2026. Hydro: the 280 MW Bad Creek pumped-storage upgrade is complete, a 50-year FERC relicense was sought on August 15, 2025 (the license expires July 2027), and Bad Creek II was deferred to 2040 in the 2025 plan. 305 MW of solar entered service in 2025. The company exited its commercial renewables business to Brookfield in 2023.

Bad Creek II second powerhouse deferred to 2040; relicense pending

productsAndServices.soldThrough: Annual competitive solar procurements (Carolinas); self-build (Florida); PPAs
productsAndServices.roadmap: Annual Carolinas solar procurement rounds; Bad Creek relicense decision before July 2027

strategyRead: (High confidence) We assess that Duke's disclosed data-center ladder is the most conservative among the large regulated utilities in this file, and that this is a reporting choice rather than a smaller business. Basis: the decks report only signed ESAs (7.8 GW), construction (5.2 GW) and a 'high-confidence, late-stage' rung (15.4 GW, inclusive of signed) with no inquiry-stage figure, where Dominion reports 53.8 GW across three rungs and AEP 69 GW of executed agreements; Duke's own Carolinas forecast counts 43 large-load projects adding 8 GW through 2035 with data centers about 80 percent of the energy. We expect the 15.4 GW to be the number the November 2026 and February 2027 calls are measured against, and the CEO has said it should convert by mid-2027.

(High confidence) We assess that Duke has bet on gas first and storage second, and that the NCUC's September 19, 2026 denial of the Smith peaker is the first evidence the bet will be adjudicated plant by plant against the same data-center load it is meant to serve. Basis: 7,501 MW of new gas in the Q2 table against ~4.5 GW of batteries by 2031; SB 266's CWIP recovery for baseload; and the commission's finding that about 70 percent of the modeled load growth behind the 255 MW turbine had 'never [been] tested in contested proceedings'. The 2025 resource-plan order due by December 31, 2026 is where the load forecast gets tested; Buck CT 3–4 and any Smith refiling depend on it.

(Moderate confidence) We assess that the large-load tariff Duke ends up with in North Carolina will sit between its own proposal (50 MW, 75 percent, 10–15 years) and the advocates' (25 MW, 85 percent, 20 years), and that Florida is the jurisdiction most likely to reject the company's first draft outright. Basis: both Carolinas settlements commit to a separate expedited proceeding before January 1, 2027 with the Public Staff as a co-author; the Florida PSC's public counsel and a commissioner have already called the DEF policy 'facially noncompliant' with SB 484 and the statewide compliant-tariff deadline was October 1, 2026. A seller pricing a Carolinas or Florida connection should assume Dominion-class minimums (85 percent) rather than Duke's opening 75 percent.

(Moderate confidence) We assess that the storage supplier decision for the 2026–2030 portfolio is either made and undisclosed or being made through the EPC channel, and that the SC 400 MW RFP and DEF's solar-sited batteries are the doors a new supplier can actually enter. Basis: no Duke release or filing read names a battery OEM for Allen, Riverbend, Knightdale, Powerline or Bartow (Allen 1 earned the 40 percent ITC plus a 10 percent energy-community adder); the company's June 30, 2026 supplier release names GE Vernova and Siemens Energy but no storage vendor; the SC RFP has a utility-ownership track that would put the OEM choice with Duke's EPC. Treat any claim that Duke has a named storage incumbent as unverified.

(Moderate confidence) We assess that the Brookfield structure — 19.7 percent of the Florida utility sold in five tranches through June 2028 with two board seats, consent rights and a put — is the template for how Duke will fund the $5–10B of Florida and Indiana upside if it materializes, and that the company's stated 'genco' evaluation in Indiana is a second version of the same idea. Basis: the March 3, 2026 8-K; the Q2 call's statement that upside capital is 'mainly Indiana and Florida'; the CEO's 'Indiana genco structure under evaluation'. Minority capital at the operating-company level keeps the holding company's 35 percent equity-funding ratio intact.

(Moderate confidence) We assess that Duke's nuclear position — eleven units being renewed to 80 years, ~300 MW of uprates, a Belews Creek early site permit and the 2024 tariff agreements with Amazon, Google, Microsoft and Nucor — is the asset most likely to distinguish it from Dominion and Southern in the hyperscalers' eyes after 2030, but that no SMR technology, customer commitment or dollar figure has been disclosed. Basis: the 2024 MOU release, the December 30, 2025 ESP filing and the NCUC's $440M development approval. The 2027 permit decision is the next observable.

(Low confidence) We assess that the coverage plan's 'Oracle 1.4 GW under construction / Google 1 GW awaiting approval' attribution to Duke, which appears in one trade-press item, is a mis-attribution of DTE Energy's two Michigan contracts. No Duke document, filing or second source carries it; it is recorded here only so the next revision does not re-import it.

policyExposure.exposure: Enacted over the governor's veto on July 29, 2025, the law removed the 70 percent-by-2030 interim carbon target (keeping 2050 neutrality), allows CWIP recovery for baseload plants where the NCUC finds savings, permits 100 percent securitization of retired coal and exempts large generation from the $500M multiyear-plan cap. EDF estimates about $87M a year of fuel-cost burden shifts from commercial and industrial to residential customers; an NCSU analysis put the added fuel cost at up to $23B through 2050.
policyExposure.mitigation: Duke cites the 2025 Carolinas Resource Plan's 2.1 percent bill CAGR and the settlements' $120M-a-year tax-credit flow-back; the DEC and DEP settlements accept 9.8 percent ROE against 10.95 percent requested.

policyExposure.exposure: Signed May 7, 2026 and effective July 2026, SB 484 requires each large-load customer to bear its full cost of service — connection, incremental transmission and generation, operations — and set an October 1, 2026 deadline for investor-owned utilities' compliant tariffs. Duke Energy Florida's refiled Large Load Customer Policy (Docket 20260064-EI) has a 20-year term and 75–85 percent take-or-pay but no rate schedule; the Office of Public Counsel and Commissioner La Rosa called it 'facially noncompliant' at the August 25–26 hearing.
policyExposure.mitigation: DEF committed to propose a large-load rate schedule in its next rate case (its 2024 settlement runs through 2027) and says any cost gap before then falls to shareholders; FPL's LLCS-1/LLCS-2 (50 MW, 85 percent load factor) effective January 1, 2026 is the in-state benchmark.

policyExposure.exposure: Duke Energy Ohio (wires-only under an electric security plan through May 2028) and Duke Energy Kentucky (generation-owning, in PJM since 2011) sit in PJM, where the July 2026 base residual auction cleared about 7 GW short of target with roughly 500 MW of new supply and FERC's chair spoke of 'alarm bells'. The Carolinas and Florida utilities are outside any RTO and Duke Energy Indiana is in MISO, so the capacity-price exposure is confined to the Midwest utilities and is not discussed in the 2026 investor presentations.
policyExposure.mitigation: Duke Energy Ohio's proposed Rate DC data-center tariff (PUCO 26-0755-EL-ATA) and Duke Energy Kentucky's June 2026 IRP; no Duke-specific FERC co-location docket found.

policyExposure.exposure: Duke is monetizing up to $3.1B of nuclear production, solar production and storage investment tax credits generated 2025–2028 under a transfer agreement announced May 4, 2026; about $600M of nuclear PTCs flowed to customers in 2025; the DEP settlement raises the customer flow-back to $120M a year for 2027–2028; Duke Energy Florida returns $50M of the Powerline battery's ITC in 2027 and expects more than $500M of ITCs from 1.4 GW of storage over ten years; Allen BESS 1 earned the 40 percent ITC plus a 10 percent energy-community adder. No Duke deck or release read mentions the 2025 federal tax law's phase-outs, the prohibited-foreign-entity rules or battery import tariffs; the forward-looking statements cite 'increased tariffs, export controls'.
policyExposure.mitigation: Tax-credit transfer agreements; the Florida large-load policy bars service to foreign-entity large loads (a customer rule, not a supply-chain one).

policyExposure.exposure: Duke signed the pledge in July 2026 and launched 'Customer Protection Plus' the same week; North Carolina's attorney general and governor asked the NCUC to make it binding, and the commission's September 19, 2026 order denying the Smith combustion turbine says any reapplication must show compliance with the pledge. A federal bill, the Ratepayer Protection Act (HR 9340, marked up July 21, 2026), would codify similar terms.
policyExposure.mitigation: Customer Protection Plus's three commitments — studies before connection, long-term agreements with security and termination charges, and revenue sharing above cost to serve.

policyExposure.exposure: Oconee (to 2053–2054) and Robinson (to 2050) hold 80-year licenses; Brunswick's application is due by end-2026 and all eleven units are to be renewed. The Belews Creek early site permit (filed December 30, 2025) is expected in 2027. About 300 MW of uprates are planned.
policyExposure.mitigation: Not applicable — the regime is an enabler; the exposure is schedule.
